data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Decentralized networks are more resilient to correlated failure not because of redundancy, but because they possess 'Organic Stack Entropy' that prevents the synchronization of failure modes.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The decentralized services converge on a 'hidden monoculture' (e.g., all using the same cloud provider's managed Kubernetes service).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The failure trigger is at a layer below the application stack (e.g., a global BGP routing error or a fundamental flaw in the IPv6 protocol).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In a large service, redundancy is typically 'homogeneous' (identical copies of the same stack), meaning a single logic bug or configuration error is replicated across all redundant nodes. A decentralized network of independent services naturally evolves heterogeneous stacks (different languages, OS versions, and libraries). This structural diversity ensures that a trigger which crashes one service (e.g., a specific TCP window size bug) is unlikely to affect others, effectively capping the maximum possible correlated failure at the percentage of the network sharing that specific stack.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
